title: Contractor-backed thinktank calls for reforms amid £258bn infra black hole

content:
Sir John Armitt

A key thinktank has called for reforms to create better conditions for private investment after calculating a £258bn black hole in meeting the country’s infrastructure needs.

The Public Private Partnership Commission (PPPC), which includes Kier and Laing O’Rourke among its members, set out a series of recommendations to the government in its first report this week.

The body, which was set up by Bradshaw Advisory and is chaired by industry stalwart Sir John Armitt, warned that delivering the National Infrastructure and Service Transformation Authority’s (NISTA) 734-project pipeline could set the taxpayer back £391bn.

It also cautioned that meeting the needs set out by the National Infrastructure Commission in 2023 – when Armitt chaired it – would require an extra £258bn of public expenditure over the next decade.

“Delivering the scale of investment needed will require public and private finance to work together, supported by partnership models that allocate risk effectively, provide investors with sufficient confidence in project viability and deliver value for the taxpayer,” said the PPPC report.

It warned: “The government’s industrial, digital and net-zero strategies will require a properly functioning and vastly improved infrastructure base, with each requiring enabling conditions, from grid capacity to digital connectivity, that do not yet exist.”

The PPPC said UK private defined-contribution pension schemes held over £1trn yet just 3 per cent of this was invested in infrastructure, compared with 14 per cent in Australia.

“The opportunity is not simply to bring more private money into infrastructure,” added the report. “Where private capital is involved, government can also draw on the expertise of investors, developers, contractors, operators and other private-sector partners to improve project development, risk allocation and delivery.”

The PPPC called for a raft of reforms to boost the amount of private capital flowing into infrastructure projects.

It said these should be designed to create smoother planning; more stable project pipelines; long-term taxation and regulatory certainty; more streamlined institutions; standardised delivery; fewer restrictions on investment; more useful accounting rules; better structuring of deals; and a less risk-averse culture in Whitehall.

Ministers should create an infrastructure-focused equivalent to the Office for Budget Responsibility, which scrutinises government tax and spending plans, urged the report.

“It should report to parliament rather than ministers, provide independent scrutiny of the infrastructure pipeline and be legally empowered to assess significant proposed changes to major capital projects,” the study said of this proposed body.

“This would not remove decisions from elected governments. It would ensure that decisions to materially alter or cancel projects expected to span two or three parliaments are subject to transparent, independent assessment of their costs and consequences.”

The PPPC said it would publish more reports in future exploring its proposed reforms in detail.

Armitt said: “I want to be clear about what this commission is arguing for, because the term ‘public-private partnership’ carries baggage and we do not intend to hide from it.

“Some past deals between the public and private sector have served the public well, others did not. But the memory of the ‘bad’ deals has choked off private investment from whole classes of infrastructure for the better part of a decade.

“Partnership done properly was never simply a finance trick. It is a delivery and governance model, a way of bringing commercial discipline and incentives, delivery expertise and long-term capital into projects early, and of putting each risk with the party best able to manage and bear it.”
